Series::square¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::square() const -> Series
Series& Series::square_()

What It Does¶

square() returns x * x elementwise.

It is a named primitive rather than x.mul(x) or x.pow(2.0) for two reasons:

  • it reads the intent directly, and

  • its backward is 2 * x, which is cheaper and more numerically direct than routing a general power rule through pow().

Unlike most of the unary math methods, square() preserves the input dtype. Squaring an int64 series gives an int64 series (subject to integer overflow), and squaring a float32 series gives float32.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series or Series& x * x elementwise, same dtype as the input. square_() overwrites the current storage.

Gradient¶

square() is differentiable, with the simplest non-trivial polynomial rule:

d/dx square(x) = 2 * x

Examples¶

Example 1. Squaring is sign-independent, so a symmetric input gives a symmetric result.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 2.0}).square());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[4.0000, 0.2500, 0.0000, 0.2500, 4.0000]

Example 2. Integer input stays integer.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({2, 3, 4}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64).square());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 9, 16]

Example 3. square() can overflow. (1e200)^2 is 1e400, out of float64 range.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({1e200}).square());

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[inf]

Example 4. The backward multiplier is 2 * x.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 3.0, 5.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

x.square().sum().reverse();

std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-4, 6, 10]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • square() keeps the input dtype, so an integer square can overflow silently and a large float square can overflow to inf. Cast to a wider type first if that is a concern.

  • For a squared magnitude of a complex series, use abs2(); for real input the two agree.

  • NaN propagates.

Summary¶

square(x) is x * x as a dtype-preserving primitive:

  • keeps int64 / float32 / float64 as-is

  • differentiable, backward multiplier 2 * x

See Also¶

  • Series::abs2: squared magnitude; identical to square() for real input, |z|^2 for complex.

  • Series::sqrt: the inverse on non-negative input.

  • Series::pow: the general power, of which square() is the 2 case with a cheaper backward.
